title: Resh
hook: rosh, head, as in Rosh Hashanah

segments.voice: Yesterday, kuf, and holiness at the edge of a field. Your line was kuf for kadosh. Which ordinary moment did you set apart? Today, the letter of the head. Day one thousand three hundred forty-eight.

When does the Jewish year begin? Still in Egypt, before the Exodus, God tells Moses and Aaron about a month in spring. In the King James words: "This month shall be unto you the beginning of months: it shall be the first month of the year to you." Spring, then, is the head of the months. And yet the Jewish New Year, Rosh Hashanah, falls in autumn, in the seventh month. In the Torah, that day is called simply the first day of the seventh month, a day of blowing the horn. So does the year begin in spring or in fall? The answer turns on one small word. Today's letter begins it.
screen: `SPRING: THE BEGINNING OF MONTHS.` → `ROSH HASHANAH IN THE SEVENTH MONTH.` → `WHERE DOES THE YEAR BEGIN?`

segments.voice: Resh. It makes an r sound, and it begins rosh, head. Rosh Hashanah is literally the head of the year. Here it is in four parts. First, the heads of the year. The Mishnah, in the tractate named for this very holiday, answers our puzzle by saying there are four new years. One in spring, for counting the reign of kings and the order of the festivals. One in late summer, for tithing animals. One in autumn, for counting years. And one in winter, for trees. A year, it turns out, can have more than one head, depending on what you're counting. Second, the beginning. From rosh comes reshit, beginning. The Torah's very first word, bereshit, in the beginning, carries it. So does a line in Psalms, in the King James words: "The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom." Wisdom, too, has a head. Third, the shape. Resh looks a lot like dalet, the door. The difference is one corner: dalet's is sharp, resh's is rounded. In the Shema, the last letter of echad, one, is a dalet, and scribes write it large. Some commentators say it's so no one mistakes it for a resh, which would turn one into acher, another. One small corner, a different meaning. Fourth, the head itself. Rosh is the part of you that goes first, that sees before the hands move. Rosh Hashanah is not only a party for a new number on the calendar. It's a day for taking stock before the year runs. A head, in this tradition, is a place to start from, and a place to think from.
screen: `ROSH: HEAD, AS IN ROSH HASHANAH.` · `THE MISHNAH: FOUR NEW YEARS.` · `RESHIT: THE BEGINNING OF WISDOM.` · `ONE CORNER: RESH OR DALET.` · then, large: `THE BEGINNING OF MONTHS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think before acting. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you'll do later today on autopilot. Replying to a message, walking into a meeting, picking up your phone the moment you're bored. Before it happens, give it a head. Ask three quiet questions: what am I about to do, why, and what would I like to come of it? Let the answers be short. Then picture yourself pausing for one breath right before you begin. If you pray, you can ask for a clear head. The bell holds the time.
Resh. The letter of rosh, head, and of reshit, beginning: the head of the year, the head of wisdom. Today's word.
Your line: resh for rosh. Today, before the thing you named, take one breath and let your head go first. Day one thousand three hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews celebrate Rosh Hashanah, the head of the year, on the first day of the seventh month, with the blowing of the shofar; the Mishnah in tractate Rosh Hashanah counts four new years for different purposes.

fork.setup: you're asked when the Jewish year begins: spring, which Exodus calls the beginning of months, or autumn, when Rosh Hashanah falls. what does the Mishnah say?
options: there are four new years, for different things.
fork.reveal: the Mishnah opens tractate Rosh Hashanah with four new years. a year can have more than one head.

original.note: Hebrew: head; also beginning or chief. The rosh of Rosh Hashanah.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rosh Hashanah means Jewish New Year, full stop.
what it means: head of the year — and the Mishnah says the year has four heads, for different things.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 12:2 makes the spring month the beginning of months; Leviticus 23:24 sets the autumn day; Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1 lists four new years.

notes: Exodus 12:2 and Psalm 111:10 quoted from KJV. Confirm.

Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1 paraphrased: 1 Nisan (kings, festivals), 1 Elul (animal tithes), 1 Tishrei (years), and the new year for trees (1 or 15 Shevat, disputed between the schools). 'Late summer' for Elul and 'winter' for Shevat given loosely. Confirm.
'In the Torah, that day is called simply the first day of the seventh month': the name Rosh Hashanah is not used for the festival in the Torah. Confirm.
Reshit and bereshit sharing the root of rosh is standard grammar; confirm.

Large dalet in echad (Deuteronomy 6:4) and the resh/acher explanation attributed to 'some commentators'. Confirm. Note: if an earlier Dalet day (1332) used the same point, a Keeper may want to swap it.
